concepts.def: Techniques such as 3D printing that build a part layer by layer from digital data, adding material only where it is needed.
Shaping techniques such as turning, milling and drilling that remove material from a larger solid block to leave the finished form.
Shaping processes in which softened or liquid material is formed inside a mould or die, suited to producing many identical components.
Permanent methods such as welding and adhesives, or temporary fastenings such as screws and bolts, used to assemble components into products.
The volume strategy chosen for manufacture - one-off, batch, mass or continuous - each suiting different levels of demand and unit cost.
Reprogrammable machines used for repetitive, precise or hazardous manufacturing tasks, providing consistent quality and the ability to run continuously.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Final Production — a core area of Design Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Final Production brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Final Production.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an additive manufacturing technique?
options: Milling on a CNC machine
3D printing a part layer by layer
Turning a bar on a lathe
Drilling a hole in sheet steel

mcqs.q: Turning a component on a lathe is an example of:
options: Additive manufacturing
Moulding
Subtractive (wasting) manufacturing
Joining

mcqs.q: Which is a typical characteristic of one-off production?
options: Very low cost per unit
Thousands of identical products per day
Fully continuous automated lines
A single unique product made by skilled labour at high unit cost

mcqs.q: A key advantage of using robots on a production line is:
options: They never require programming or maintenance
They make every product unique
Consistent, repeatable accuracy on repetitive tasks
They eliminate the need for quality systems
Yes - robots also design the products they make.
Yes - 3D printers carve the shape out of a block of plastic.
No - 3D printing is additive: it deposits material layer by layer, whereas subtractive processes cut material away from a solid block.
Yes - 3D printing is a type of injection moulding.

mcqs.q: Is mass production always the cheapest way to make a product?
options: Yes - robots also design the products they make.
Yes - mass production is always cheaper than any other scale.
Yes - because mass-produced items never need quality checks.
No - mass production gives a low unit cost only at high volumes; for small quantities, the huge tooling and set-up costs make one-off or batch production cheaper overall.

mcqs.q: Do robots in automated production remove the need for human workers entirely?
options: No - humans are still needed to program, supervise and maintain robots, manage quality systems and handle non-routine problems.
Yes - a fully automated factory needs no human involvement at all.
Yes - robots also design the products they make.
Yes - 3D printing is a type of injection moulding.
